summary: Describes a way for Proxy Mobile IPv6 to choose a local mobility anchor at runtime, during the exchange of Proxy Binding Update and Acknowledgement messages. A use for this is balancing load across anchors.

plainLanguage.summary: A device moving around needs a home base to forward its traffic. This lets the network choose a base on the spot, such as the least busy one, instead of fixing it ahead of time.

questions: what is an rflma and r2lma
subtitle: Lets a Proxy Mobile IPv6 anchor hand a device's session to a better anchor while the first binding exchange is still happening.

tldr.problem: In Proxy Mobile IPv6, the anchor a gateway first contacts, chosen through DNS or AAA, may not be the best one at that moment, and DNS or AAA data cannot track anchor load closely.
tldr.mechanism: The contacted anchor (the rfLMA) answers the Proxy Binding Update with a Redirect option naming another anchor (the r2LMA) where the session was created. The gateway then talks to the r2LMA directly.
tldr.outcome: Anchors can be chosen at runtime, for example to balance load, without extra signaling to set up and tear down a session on the wrong anchor.

today: RFC 6463 is a Proposed Standard from February 2012. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why Runtime Assignment
sections.content:
This RFC adds a way for Proxy Mobile IPv6 (PMIPv6, RFC 5213) to assign a local mobility anchor (LMA) at runtime. The assignment happens during the Proxy Binding Update (PBU) and Proxy Binding Acknowledgement (PBA) exchange between a mobile access gateway (MAG) and an LMA. It does not depend on DNS or AAA for choosing the anchor, and all MAGs and LMAs must be in the same PMIPv6 domain.

The RFC gives several reasons. A cluster or blade-style LMA can appear as several LMAs with separate addresses, so the MAG's first choice may be suboptimal. A load-balancer in front of a cluster can become a bottleneck if all traffic goes through it, so bypassing it after the first PBU/PBA exchange helps scalability. DNS-based and AAA-based selection are hard to keep current with LMA load because of caching and zone update delays. Finally, the base PMIPv6 specification does not say how to treat IPv6 anycast addresses on mobility agents.

The RFC concludes that DNS and AAA approaches cannot select an appropriate LMA at runtime, which is the gap this specification fills.
sections.plainLanguage: Looking up a helper in a phone book is slow and out of date. It is better if the helper you call can tell you right away who is least busy.

sections.title: Roles and Assumptions
sections.content:
Two new roles appear. The rfLMA is the LMA that receives a PBU from a MAG and decides to assign the session to another LMA. The r2LMA is the LMA that ends up serving the MAG. A runtime assignment domain is a group of LMAs with at least one rfLMA and one or more r2LMAs, all in the same PMIPv6 domain. An rfLMA may only assign MAGs to r2LMAs in its own runtime assignment domain.

Each LMA MUST be reachable at a unicast IP address. The rfLMA and r2LMA MUST have a prior agreement, adequate means to secure their communication and an established trust relationship. MAGs and LMAs are assumed to have the required Security Associations pre-established; dynamic negotiation, for example with IKEv2, SHOULD be supported but is out of scope.
sections.plainLanguage: The first helper you reach is the front-desk helper. The one who actually takes your case is the second helper. They must already know and trust each other.

sections.title: The New Mobility Options
sections.content:
The RFC defines four mobility options, all in network byte order. They are registered in the Mobility Options registry as 46 to 49.

  • Redirect-Capability (46): sent by the MAG in a PBU to say it supports and has enabled runtime assignment. Option Length MUST be 2. At most one per PBU.
  • Redirect (47): sent by the LMA in a PBA to carry the r2LMA's unicast address. The K flag means an IPv6 address is present and the N flag means an IPv4 address is present; exactly one is set. The address family MUST match the transport between the MAG and the rfLMA.
  • Load Information (48): can be in any PBA. It carries a Priority (lower value means higher priority), Sessions in Use, Maximum Sessions, Used Capacity and Maximum Capacity, the capacities in kilobytes per second. A MAG MAY use it to keep a priority ordering of LMAs.
  • Alternate IPv4 Care-of Address (49): the IPv4 counterpart of the Alternate Care-of Address option of RFC 6275. An LMA that implements it MUST echo it back in the PBA.
sections.plainLanguage: There are four small labels. One says 'I can be redirected', one says 'go see this other helper', one says 'here is how busy I am', and one holds a spare address.

sections.title: How the Assignment Works
sections.content:
A MAG that supports and has enabled the feature includes Redirect-Capability in a PBU that creates a new session (Handoff Indicator value 1). Assignment concerns one mobility session at a time. If the rfLMA decides to assign, it replies with a PBA that has a success status and a Redirect option holding the r2LMA's unicast address. The PBA still comes from the address the PBU was sent to, the rfLMA address. The rfLMA MUST NOT change the transport address family.

If the MAG gets a Redirect option in a PBA after offering Redirect-Capability, it updates its Binding Update List Entry to the r2LMA address, and if there is no SA with the r2LMA it SHOULD try to create one dynamically. It does not need to send a fresh PBU, because the session already exists in the r2LMA. All user traffic and later PBUs (lifetime extension, handoff and so on) go to the r2LMA, and the MAG creates a tunnel if none exists. If the MAG did not offer Redirect-Capability, it MUST ignore a Redirect option.

If the rfLMA has the feature enabled but will not assign and will not serve as a normal LMA, it MUST reject the PBU with Status Value 130 (Insufficient resources).
sections.plainLanguage: You tell the first helper you are happy to be passed on. They pass you on and tell you the new helper's name, and from then on you only talk to the new one.

sections.title: Two Deployment Models
sections.content:
The RFC describes two ways to arrange the rfLMA and r2LMA, and says that any arrangement works as long as the MAG-to-rfLMA protocol follows this specification.

Co-located. The rfLMA and r2LMAs are parts of one LMA. The rfLMA is reachable at an anycast or loopback address and each r2LMA at its own unicast address. On a PBU with Redirect-Capability, the co-located LMA creates the session in the r2LMA role using the RFC 5213 procedures and sends a PBA from the rfLMA address with the r2LMA address in the Redirect option. A PBU sent to the r2LMA unicast address gets a normal PBA with no Redirect option.

Separate (proxy-MAG). The rfLMA acts as a non-transparent proxy-MAG: an LMA toward the real MAG and a base RFC 5213 MAG toward the r2LMA. It creates only proxy state, picks an r2LMA, and sends a new PBU' with the original non-security options plus an Alternate Care-of Address option holding the original MAG's Proxy Care-of Address (the A4CoA option for IPv4 transport, RFC 5844). The r2LMA can be an ordinary RFC 5213 or RFC 5844 LMA that does not know this specification, except that for IPv4 it MUST implement the Alternate IPv4 Care-of Address option.

When the PBA' arrives, the rfLMA sends the MAG a PBA with the Redirect option, copies other non-security options (including Load Information) and then removes the proxy state. If the r2LMA fails or does not answer, the rfLMA SHOULD try another r2LMA according to local policy; if all fail it returns the last Status Value, or 130 if no response.
sections.plainLanguage: Either the two helpers sit in the same office and one simply hands you over, or the front-desk helper phones the second helper for you, then tells you the answer and steps out of the way.

sections.title: Multi-Homing and Configuration
sections.content:
A multi-homed mobile node that wants handovers between interfaces needs one LMA controlling all its sessions. The RFC's supported approach is to apply runtime assignment only on the first attach, store the assigned r2LMA address in the policy profile, and reuse it for later sessions without contacting the rfLMA. This relies on the node having an identity that always points to the same profile. How policy information is shared among MAGs is deployment specific.

Two configuration variables control the feature, both defaulting to FALSE. EnableLMARedirectFunction is available in a MAG and in an rfLMA. EnableLMARedirectAcceptFunction is available in an r2LMA and lets it accept sessions assigned by an rfLMA.
sections.plainLanguage: If you use two devices, the network remembers which helper you got the first time and sends the second device to the same helper.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The security considerations of RFC 5213 apply. A misconfigured LMA could try to assign MAGs to non-existent LMAs or to LMAs that will not have an SA with the MAG, causing failed binding updates or failed sessions, and could bias load distribution in the domain. The RFC assumes that participating LMAs have adequate prior agreement and trust.

If MAG-LMA SAs are manually keyed, the anti-replay service of ESP-protected traffic cannot typically be provided. If an rfLMA must modify a PBU or PBA, for example by changing the outer IP addresses, the protection used MUST NOT cover those parts of the outer packet. Alternatively the rfLMA can do all security processing and the rfLMA-to-r2LMA traffic is unprotected at the PMIPv6 level, in which case the domain MUST provide adequate security by other means such as layer-2 VPNs.
sections.plainLanguage: If a helper points you to the wrong place, your request just fails, so the helpers must be set up carefully and trust each other.

messages.note: rfLMA picks an r2LMA and creates proxy state.

messages.label: PBU'
messages.note: Carries the MAG's Proxy Care-of Address.

messages.label: PBA + Redirect
messages.note: Names the r2LMA; proxy state removed.
